identification.summary: China-based espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Mulberry Typhoon (formerly MANGANESE) and that Mandiant and MITRE track as APT5 [S1][S8][S9]. MITRE says it primarily targets the telecommunications, aerospace and defense industries in the U.S., Europe and Asia and has a strong interest in compromising networking devices and their software, including with zero-day exploits [S8]. Microsoft reported in 2023 that Mulberry Typhoon targeted the US defense industrial base, most notably with a zero-day exploit against devices (CVE-2022-27518) [S1]. In December 2022 NSA published threat-hunting guidance on APT5's exploitation of Citrix ADC [S4][S5].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2007 [S8]. 2019 press coverage of FireEye reporting also says the group has been active since 2007 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Mulberry Typhoon (formerly MANGANESE) [S1][S9]. MITRE associates Mulberry Typhoon, MANGANESE, BRONZE FLEETWOOD, Keyhole Panda and UNC2630 with APT5 [S8]. NSA-related coverage calls APT5 also UNC2630 and MANGANESE [S4][S6]. Mandiant itself only assessed UNC2630 as possibly tied to APT5, based on a trusted third party's evidence that it could not independently confirm [S2]. 2019 coverage of FireEye reporting describes APT5 as several subgroups with distinct tactics and infrastructure [S7].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (suspected). Mandiant suspected UNC2630 operates on behalf of the Chinese government [S2]. Its May 2021 update says UNC2630 and UNC2717 are believed to be affiliated with the Chinese government [S3]. Coverage of the NSA guidance calls APT5 a Chinese state-sponsored group [S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes Mulberry Typhoon as China-based [S1]. NSA publicly attributed the CVE-2022-27518 exploitation to APT5 in December 2022, according to press coverage of the advisory [S4][S5]. Mandiant held the UNC2630 to APT5 link at low-to-moderate confidence ('may have ties'; 'not able to definitively connect') [S2]. 2019 coverage notes that FireEye had not formally attributed APT5 to a nation-state [S7].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and reporting [S1]; Mandiant incident response at Pulse Secure victims, plus third-party linkage to historic APT5 campaigns [S2][S3]; NSA threat-hunting guidance, which this record relies on through press reporting [S4][S5][S6]; MITRE ATT&CK group entry [S8].

objectives: Espionage aimed at defense, aerospace and telecommunications targets [S1][S8]. Mandiant judged that Pulse Secure-era activity sought to steal credentials, keep long-term persistent access to victim networks and access or exfiltrate sensitive data, in support of key Chinese government priorities [S3]. Earlier VPN-exploitation coverage reported spying on pricing and bidding information [S7].

sectors: Government, high tech, education, transportation and financial (broader Pulse Secure campaign, not UNC2630 alone) [S3]
targeting.notes: Microsoft groups Mulberry Typhoon with Circle Typhoon and Volt Typhoon as China-based groups targeting the US DIB. It says their targets occasionally overlap but they are distinct actors with different infrastructure and capabilities [S1]. Mandiant's May 2021 sector list covers the whole Pulse Secure campaign (UNC2630 and UNC2717) [S3].

capabilities.summary: Exploits edge and network appliances, including zero-days: Pulse Secure CVE-2021-22893 alongside older flaws [S2], Citrix ADC/Gateway CVE-2022-27518 [S1][S4], and, per 2019 coverage, Pulse Secure CVE-2019-11510 and Fortinet CVE-2018-13379 [S7]. CVE-2022-27518 allowed unauthenticated remote code execution on appliances configured as a SAML SP or IdP [S4]. UNC2630 deployed purpose-built Pulse Secure implants: SLOWPULSE, which modifies legitimate Pulse Secure files to bypass or log credentials in authentication flows, including some 2FA, plus RADIALPULSE, THINBLOOD, ATRIUM, PACEMAKER, SLIGHTPULSE and PULSECHECK [S2]. Later families include BLOODMINE, BLOODBANK, CLEANPULSE and RAPIDPULSE [S3]. Operators patched devices for persistence that survived upgrades, removed webshells to evade detection and cleared logs [S3]. MITRE also lists Mimikatz, Skeleton Key, PoisonIvy, gh0st RAT and PcShare [S8].

campaigns.name: SSL VPN pre-auth file-read exploitation (Pulse Secure, Fortinet)
campaigns.summary: Press reporting says APT5 began exploiting CVE-2019-11510 and CVE-2018-13379 to steal files containing credentials and VPN session data.

campaigns.name: Pulse Secure Connect intrusions against the US DIB (UNC2630)
campaigns.summary: From August 2020 to March 2021, UNC2630 used CVE-2021-22893 and earlier flaws with SLOWPULSE and related implants against US DIB companies. Mandiant noted a possible APT5 tie.

campaigns.name: UNC2630 webshell cleanup and persistence
campaigns.summary: Between 17 and 20 April 2021, UNC2630 accessed dozens of compromised devices and removed webshells, in one case leaving a persistence patcher in place. Mandiant then reported four new families.

campaigns.name: Citrix ADC/Gateway zero-day CVE-2022-27518
campaigns.summary: NSA released 'APT5: Citrix ADC Threat Hunting Guidance' as Citrix patched an actively exploited unauthenticated RCE. Microsoft later cited this zero-day for Mulberry Typhoon.

campaigns.name: Microsoft East Asia report names Mulberry Typhoon
campaigns.summary: Microsoft lists Mulberry Typhoon among China-based groups targeting the US defense industrial base.

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage operators tracked as Mulberry Typhoon/APT5. UNC2630 is a possibly related Mandiant cluster [S1][S2][S8].
diamond.capability: Zero-day and n-day exploits for VPN and application-delivery appliances; trojanized appliance binaries (SLOWPULSE family); webshells; credential theft; log tampering [S2][S3][S4][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised edge appliances (Pulse Secure, Citrix ADC, Fortinet) serve as access and persistence points [S2][S4][S7]. Microsoft says Mulberry Typhoon's infrastructure is distinct from that of Circle and Volt Typhoon [S1].
diamond.victim: US defense industrial base, aerospace and telecommunications companies (including satellite communications) and technology firms in the U.S., Europe and Asia [S1][S2][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection supporting key Chinese government priorities against Western defense and telecom sectors [S1][S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing SSL VPN and ADC appliances with SAML or authentication roles, which sit outside EDR coverage and have limited forensic visibility [S2][S3][S4].

gaps: The NSA advisory 'APT5: Citrix ADC Threat Hunting Guidance' (December 2022) could not be opened; its content is cited through press coverage [S4][S5][S6].
No Microsoft report dedicated to Mulberry Typhoon was found. Microsoft's public description is limited to the 2023 East Asia report [S1].
Original FireEye reporting on APT5's 2007 origins and subgroups was not retrieved; it is cited through 2019 press coverage [S7].
The UNC2630 to APT5 link rests on an unnamed third party per Mandiant [S2]. Some press coverage overstates it as confirmed; treat Pulse Secure-era facts as UNC2630, not as definitively APT5.
Microsoft says Mulberry, Circle and Volt Typhoon targets overlap, but finds insufficient evidence to tie the groups together [S1].
No 2024-2026 public reporting attributing new activity to Mulberry Typhoon or APT5 was found in this research pass.
The vendor sources gathered here do not substantiate the CrowdStrike (Keyhole Panda) and Secureworks (BRONZE FLEETWOOD) alias mappings beyond MITRE's listing [S8].
No sponsoring organization (MSS, PLA or contractor) is named in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the edge: SSL VPN concentrators, Citrix ADC/Gateway and SAML-integrated access appliances on DIB, aerospace and telecom networks that connect to DoD programs [S1][S2][S4]. STEP 2: These appliances often fall outside EDR coverage and retain few logs. The actor patches appliance binaries and clears logs, so absence of evidence is weak [S2][S3]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is appliance exploit (zero-day or fresh n-day), then trojanized authentication components or a webshell, then credential harvest, then internal access and data staging [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, long-term credential theft and data collection from DIB and telecom networks via edge devices [S3]. MDCOA is a rapid mass-exploitation wave against a newly discovered appliance zero-day across DoD-adjacent contractors, with implants that survive vendor patching and upgrades, giving persistent access to program data during a crisis [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: modified Pulse Secure or Citrix system files and integrity-check failures, unexpected webshells on appliances, gaps or truncation in appliance logs, and authentication successes that bypass MFA [S2][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: JCC2 should track edge-appliance inventory and patch state, plus vendor integrity-check results, for DoD and mission-partner networks, because this actor's entry point is the appliance [S2][S4]. (2) Authorities: most observed victims are DIB companies [S1][S2]. Response depends on DC3/DIB CS sharing, CISA and NSA advisories and contractor cooperation rather than DoD-owned terrain. (3) Mission assurance: an appliance patch alone does not remove a persistence patcher [S3]. Plan for rebuild or replacement and credential resets on systems behind compromised appliances. (4) Coordination: Mulberry, Circle and Volt Typhoon target the same DIB sector but are distinct actors [S1]. Deconflict hunts and reporting by actor, and avoid merging indicators across clusters.

provenance.importedSummary: APT5 is a China-based espionage actor that has been active since at least 2007 primarily targeting the telecommunications, aerospace, and defense industries throughout the U.S., Europe, and Asia. APT5 has displayed advanced tradecraft and significant interest in compromising networking devices and their underlying software including through the use of zero-day exploits.
